title: Search inside a client portal
metaTitle: Search that finds the promised file
excerpt: Clients search a portal when folder names fail them. Show the file in the words they were promised, with the date and who updated it, and a way back to that folder.
alt: A glass-walled office corridor with a sofa, a floor lamp, and black pendant lights, a hallway of similar doors that needs a name to tell them apart.
caption: When the rooms look alike, the name on the door has to match the name they were given. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Why do clients search a portal?
faqs.answer: They search when the folders failed them. The folder was named for an internal phase, the email used a different title than the file, or three versions exist and they cannot tell which is current. Search is the repair. It should speak the words from the email, not only the words from the studio's filing system.

faqs.question: What should a portal search result include?
faqs.answer: Include the human title, the filename, the project, the date, and who updated it, and mark the current version if older ones remain. Say if it is view only. A row with only an icon and a slug makes them open the wrong file before a meeting, so the match should be obvious before the tap.

faqs.question: What if their search matches nothing?
faqs.answer: Repeat the query and name the project you looked in. Offer the nearest current file if there is one, labeled as a suggestion, not as a fake match. Do not show another client's files to fill the gap. Do not dump every file in the project under an empty message and call it helpful.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Client portal search UX is the repair when a folder name failed a client who is looking for the file they were promised. Show matches in their language. Show a way back to the folder they already trusted. If you cannot do those two things, the search box is a second maze.

They type "logo," "brand guidelines," or the phrase from your email. They do not type your phase name. A portal that only matches "Sprint 4 / export / final" will tell them the file does not exist. They will believe it, and they will ask for a resend you do not need to make.

## They search because the folders failed

Folders fail when they are named for the studio's process. Discovery. Sprint. Handoff. The client remembers the thing: the logo pack, the contract, the homepage copy. If the first screen already showed that file, they may never search. Search is for the day the first screen is a long archive and the email is three weeks old.

Put the field at the top of the project, labeled Search files. Placeholder text can say "Logo pack" as an example they might type. Do not make them choose a file type before they can search. Type filters are how a PDF hides from someone who does not remember it was a PDF.

Scope the search to their projects only, and default it to the project they are in. A global box that jumps to another project without saying so feels like you reshuffled the room. If a result is from another of their projects, label the project on the row. They should never see a third client's title, even as a "did you mean."

Jakob Nielsen wrote that people often leave in 10 to 20 seconds if the page does not show its value immediately. Search results are that page. [How long people stay on a page](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) argues for a first row that looks like the file from the email, not a help article about how search works.

## Matches in the words you already used

Index the human title, the filename, and the words from the note you attached when you shared it. If the email said "brand guidelines" and the file is "Hanabi_Northwind_Guidelines_v3.pdf," both phrases should hit. You do not need to show the ugly filename as the only title. You do need to match it, because some clients will type what they downloaded last time.

Each row shows the title, the date, who updated it, and whether it is the current version. Those four facts prevent the wrong file from going into a deck. Highlight the matching words if you want. Do not hide the date. A logo with no date is how last month's mark gets presented as this month's.

If a file is view only, the row carries the same sentence as the file list. Search is not a side door around permissions. If a file is not shared with this person, it does not appear, and the snippet does not quote it. Test snippets. Snippets are a common leak because they are rendered by a different query than the list.

Group current files above retired ones, or badge the retired ones so clearly that a hurried person will not tap them first. A relevance sort that prefers an older file because it matches more words is a bad sort for a portal. Current beats slightly more relevant. Say so in the row, not in a legend.

People and comments can be results only if the client would look for them that way. A comment that says "use this logo" might be how they remember the file. If you include comments, label them as comments and show the file they sit on. Do not make a comment look like a file. They will try to download it.

## A way back to the folder

The query stays in the field. They will add a word. Clearing it when they submit makes them retype "guidelines" on a phone outside your office. Keep it.

If they opened search from a folder, the way back names that folder. "Back to Brand." Returning should restore the folder, not a root dashboard. The folder was the last place they understood. Search was the detour.

Opening a result and going back should restore the same results and the same query. Losing the query after a wrong open means they must remember what they typed. They will not. They will email you.

If you suggest a spelling fix, offer it. Do not replace "logopack" silently. "Search logo pack instead" under their words is respectful. Silent replacement that finds nothing, because you "fixed" the query into something else that also misses, is infuriating and hard to see.

Do not add a search history that shows sensitive filenames on a shared computer without a way to clear it. A client portal often sits on a laptop in a conference room. Recent searches of contract names are not a convenience feature. Keep history to the session, or let them turn it off in settings. The cabinet is the next article. Search should already have a safe default.

## Nothing matched

Repeat the query and the scope. "No files in Brand match 'wordmark.'" That proves you looked where they thought you looked. "No results" does not say where.

If a current file is close, offer it as a suggestion with its real title. "Closest current file: Logo pack, Tuesday." They can accept it. Do not quietly list it as if it matched. Dishonest rows train people to distrust the ones that are exact.

If the file exists but is not shared yet, do not hint at the secret title. "Nothing you can open matches that" is the line. The studio's view can show that a match exists and is invisible to the client, so you know to share it. The client's view stays quiet.

Do not pad the empty state with every file in the project. They came to narrow the world. Widening it to the full tree is the folder problem again. A link back to the folder is the right second action. The folder is browse. The empty search should admit it found nothing, then point at browse on purpose.

If they searched from the wrong project, and another of their projects has the file, you may say the project name. "A file named logo pack is in the other project, Northwind." Only if they are allowed to see that project. Never across clients. Never as a preview of the file's contents.


## Versions, previews, and the file they meant

Search is where an old version ambushes a client. They remember a phrase that lives in the retired file and not in the current one, so the old file ranks first. Badge it as retired before the title, not after a name that may be cut off on a phone. Show the current file in the same group even if the query matched it less perfectly, and badge that one as current. They can still open the old file for the record. They should have to choose it on purpose, with the badge in view before the tap.

Preview and download on the result have to match the file row. If the file is view only, the result must not offer a download that the file then refuses. That mismatch is a permission bug wearing a search icon. Use one row component in both places. Two templates will drift the week someone is rushing to ship the search field, and the client will be the one who finds the drift, usually from a lobby.

If the match is a comment, show enough of the comment to recognize it and put the file title above it. Do not show a comment that quotes a file this person can no longer access. Check access when you render the snippet, not only when you index. Indexes go stale. A stale snippet is a leak that the folder view will not reveal, because the folder is already correct.
## Review it with the email in your hand

Take five phrases from real emails you have sent. The casual name. The filename. A word from the cover note. An old version's name. A word that should miss.

Run them as the client, on a phone. The current file should be obvious. View only should be obvious. Back should return to the folder you started in, query intact. Run the same phrases as a different client and confirm the rows are empty of anything that is not theirs, including snippets.

Open a result that is a retired version and confirm you can tell before you download. If you cannot, the badge is too quiet for the meeting they are about to walk into.

Settings are where they decide who else can see files and whether they are told when a file changes. That cabinet is next, [settings in a client portal](/blog/settings-in-a-client-portal). Search that ignores a revoked teammate is a permission bug you will not see in the folder view.

If search should return the file you named in the email, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The work includes the handoff. A client who can find the file does not need a second email with the same attachment.
